title: Repertoire, tempo, and ballyhoo advertising
summary: They played tradition not Dixieland, read sheet music, and advertised dances by truck ballyhoo.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: Did you have to play any differently for the people in the country, you know like in Pensacola, than you did? No.

We played our one star, which we all called it. It's what they called tradition, not Dixieland. But we did have reading music, reading musicians, because why we made it better than the other guys, because we could go by the sheet music and learn the songs. In those days when the songs were changing quite a bit, and if the bands didn't learn no songs, the people wouldn't hire them. And if you didn't play the right tempo for them people to dance, the man wouldn't hire you. But we understood all that. And learn how to get along with people and make yourself pleasant with people, you see, make people like you, you see. And they used to do the same thing like I just said in Pensacola Mobile, when you all in there, you had black clubs, organizations around you, and you had to go to Ballyhoo. You had to go advertise on the truck. You used to use a furniture wagon. That's how they called it a tailgate ramble in there, oh they did. Then they went to Automobile, little trucks putting you on. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

Then they went to automobiles, little trucks, put in your arms. And they had radio that had come out, but everybody didn't have a radio. They used to use it for, not only the music, new chords would come out. They used to use bands to go down and ballyhoo, let the people know the new chords would be out and everything. See, it was quite a few people to work. And then of course I didn't play in the funeral none of that because I wasn't a brass or a reas. Had a lot of organizations that had already contracted for the people that died, they'd have a funeral with a band with them. You see they had them all in the football city city. How you could do that. And they had a lot of dancing places, small and large and everything. So there was a lot of work, not only in yards and other places, wherever we went, where I went.
When you were advertising, what, if you were playing a dance at night, you would go around in a furniture wagon or in a car and play, a truck, you know, and play throughout the city?

No, you had certain areas you went into. You couldn't call it where the hall was. You would go to approximately, let's see, twelve or twenty-four blocks in the area, or twelve, in that area. Because, I mean like uptown, back of town, or front of town, if it was in that area, you would go around Balli-Hood in that area, you see. And the people liked the way the band sounded when it was Balli-Hood, they'd come to the dance. If they knew the musicians, the people that went to dance, they knew a lot of the musicians, black and white, they knew. They'd come to the dance. And then in your age, you had your time, your season, your elect season, most everything dropped down slowly, you see. But right after Lent, everything's opened up, you see. So, like I said, that was the slowest part of the year, Lent. Well, the British people were Catholic, they'd go to the dance, you see. Yeah, that's a wonderful thing, man. So, like I said, you have to, music is just like any kind of trade or business you have. You're competitors all around. You like to build yourself up to be popular and do things to please the public. And if you, like I said, the band that didn't, people would try them out. And if they didn't have that flow dancing, that man would get another band.
